title: Commercial Christmas Decorations Budget: A Planning Guide for Canada
metaDescription: Plan a commercial Christmas decorations budget in Canada: per-pole, per-tree and per-entrance cost ranges, install labour, power, storage and a 3-season plan.
excerpt: Malls, BIAs and municipalities rarely overspend on the decorations themselves. The overruns come from labour, power, storage and replacement. This guide gives CAD planning ranges per pole, tree and entrance, plus a three-season phasing model.
heroAlt: Commercial pole-mount snowflake decorations and lit street trees on a Canadian main street at dusk
keyTakeaways: Budget by unit (per pole, per tree, per entrance) so you can scale the plan up or down without redoing the maths.
Install labour, lift rental and takedown often add 20 to 35 percent on top of the product cost in year one.
Operating electricity for a full LED display is small; wiring, transformers and electrician time are not.
Phase a large display over three seasons, starting with the highest-traffic nodes, and buy reusable core pieces first.
Reserve 8 to 12 percent of the display value each year for spares, repairs and storage supplies.

body.text: Most commercial Christmas decoration budgets go wrong the same way: someone prices the decorations and forgets everything around them. The lit snowflake is on the quote, but the bucket truck, the electrician, the transformer enclosures, the storage racking and next year's replacement bulbs are not. This guide breaks a display into units you can count, gives realistic CAD planning ranges for each, and shows how to phase the purchase over three seasons so the first year looks good without committing the whole capital budget.

All dollar figures in this guide are planning ranges for budget approval, not quotes. Final pricing depends on size, quantity, shipping distance and volume. Submit your item list through the [quote request](/request-a-quote) and the team replies with line-item pricing, usually within one business day.
Start with a count, not a number
Before you set a total, walk the site and count what can actually be decorated. A defensible budget starts from a unit list, not from last year's spend plus a percentage.

items: Light poles with usable mounting height and an existing or nearby power source (count them, then mark which are on the primary pedestrian route).
Trees that can be wrapped: trunk diameter, canopy height and whether crews can reach them without closing a lane.
Entrances, archways, canopies and storefront bays that deserve a feature piece.
Open spaces suitable for one photo-op display, a lit tree or a walk-through feature.
Roofline, fascia or railing runs measured in feet, which decide how many C9 spools you need.

body.text: Once you have the counts, assign each unit a tier: signature (high traffic, premium piece), standard (repeating pole or tree treatment) or accent (simple garland, wreath or bow). A typical Canadian main street ends up around 15 percent signature, 60 percent standard and 25 percent accent.
Planning ranges per unit in CAD

These ranges reflect commercial-grade product, meaning aluminum frames, IP44-rated 24V low-voltage LED sets and UV-treated foliage. They exclude installation and freight. Use them to rough in a budget, then replace them with actual quotes.

items: Pole-mount decor: a 3 to 4 ft lit pole-mount snowflake, star or candy cane typically lands between $450 and $800; a 5 ft piece typically lands between $900 and $1,300. Browse the [pole-mount decor range](/product-category/pole-mount-decor) for sizes.
Tree wraps: lighting a mature street tree with 5mm mini lights typically costs $150 to $400 in product, depending on trunk wrap versus full canopy. See mini lights.
Entrance or photo-op feature: a 3D lit archway, gift box or ornament ring typically runs $2,500 to $6,500. See [3D displays](/product-category/3d) and photo-op displays.
Overhead span: a 40 ft street-crossing message typically runs $3,000 to $7,500, plus engineered anchor points. See [overhead and skyline decor](/product-category/overhead-skyline-decor).

Wreaths, garland and bows: a 4 to 6 ft commercial wreath often falls in the $200 to $600 range; 10 ft garland sections and structural bows are priced per piece and vary by size. See wreaths and garlands and commercial bows.
Roofline C9 lighting: budget by the foot. One bulb per foot at 12-inch spacing means a 200 ft roofline needs 200 bulbs, and C9 LED bulbs start from $45 for a 25-pack. See C9 LED bulbs.

body.text: Install labour, lifts and takedown

Labour is where first-year budgets slip. A two-person crew with a bucket truck can usually mount a pole piece in 10 to 15 minutes once the layout is marked and the hardware is staged, but travel between poles, traffic control and power hookups stretch that to a realistic 4 to 6 poles per hour on a busy street. Budget roughly 20 to 35 percent of product cost for first-year installation, less if pieces share brackets from prior years.
Staff crew or contractor

Municipal parks and public works crews often install pole decor themselves, because they already own the lift and the traffic permits. BIAs and malls usually hire a contractor. If you hire, ask for separate line items for install, takedown, mid-season service calls and storage handling, so you can compare against a professional installer quote on equal terms.
Do not forget takedown
Takedown costs about 60 to 70 percent of installation, because there is no layout work but pieces must be inspected, tagged and packed. Budget it now, not in January.
Electricity and wiring

LED displays are cheap to run and expensive to wire. At a planning rate of about 15 cents per kWh, 100 pole pieces drawing an average of 100 W for 6 hours a night over 45 nights use roughly 2,700 kWh, or about $400. That is a rounding error next to the electrician's invoice.

items: Sum nameplate watts per circuit and keep continuous load under 80 percent of breaker rating: 12 A on a 15 A circuit, or 1,440 W at 120V.
Place 24V transformers in weatherproof, lockable enclosures and keep the low-voltage runs short; voltage drop shows up as dim ends on long runs.
Use a timer or photocell per circuit so the display runs dusk to a set hour, which also trims the power bill.
Confirm who owns each power source before you design around it: many pole outlets belong to the utility, not the municipality.
Stock extension cords and wire and accessories such as clips, timers and connectors as a line item, not an afterthought.

body.text: Storage, repair and replacement

A display that is purchased once and stored badly is a three-year display. Plan storage as a physical footprint: a 4 ft pole piece needs roughly the floor space of a pallet slot per 4 to 6 pieces when racked, and large 3D pieces need their own bays. Label every piece with its pole location so next year's install is a matching exercise, not a puzzle.

items: Reserve 8 to 12 percent of display value per year for spare bulbs, transformers, brackets and repairs.
Test every lit piece in November, not in storage in January, and tag failures for warranty or repair before the season closes.
Keep a shared spreadsheet of piece IDs, locations, transformer pairings and the date of last test.

body.text: Phasing a display over three seasons
Few organizations fund a full display at once, and a phased plan lets you prove value to council, members or ownership before the next ask.
Season one: core and landmarks

Buy the signature pieces and the standard pole decor for the busiest block or entrance. Aim for roughly 40 percent of the total plan. Pick durable, non-dated designs that will still fit a different layout next year.
Season two: extend and connect
Add the next 35 percent: more poles, tree wraps and a photo-op display. Use season-one usage data, such as foot traffic counts and social media tags, to decide where the extra pieces go.
Season three: fill and refresh
Complete the plan with the final 25 percent, and rotate in one new theme piece. From season four onward, the line item becomes a steady maintenance and refresh budget instead of a capital ask.

Ordering early matters more than most budgets admit. Commercial decor ships from Holiday Light Supplies in London, Ontario, and large 3D and overhead pieces need lead time. Submit inquiries by September for installs in mid-November, and free shipping applies to orders over $150.
Worked example: a 30-pole main street
To see how the ranges stack up, take a small downtown with 30 usable poles, 12 street trees and one photo-op location. Using the planning ranges above, the product line looks like this.

items: 30 standard 3 to 4 ft pole-mount pieces at $450 to $800 each: $13,500 to $24,000.
12 tree wraps at $150 to $400 each: $1,800 to $4,800.
One 3D photo-op feature: $2,500 to $6,500.
Product subtotal: roughly $17,800 to $35,300.
Installation at 20 to 35 percent of product cost, plus takedown at 60 to 70 percent of that: roughly $5,700 to $21,000.
Annual spares and repair reserve at 8 to 12 percent: roughly $1,400 to $4,200.

body.text: That puts the first-year total at roughly $25,000 to $60,500 before electrical work and storage. The wide spread is the point: the low end assumes municipal crews, existing outlets and reused brackets, while the high end assumes contractor labour, new circuits and traffic control. Narrow the range by getting two things confirmed early: who installs, and where the power comes from.
Where to cut without hurting the display

When the first total comes back above what ownership or council will approve, resist the urge to thin out every block equally. A display with gaps reads as unfinished. These levers usually work better.

items: Cover fewer blocks fully rather than all blocks partially, and extend next season.
Swap one premium 3D feature for a repeating pole design that the street already uses.
Choose warm white C9 roofline lighting and mini-light tree wraps for visual impact at a lower cost per foot than large custom pieces.
Ask for volume pricing: quantities of identical pole pieces usually price better than a mix of designs.
Reuse brackets and transformers across years by standardizing on one piece size per block.

body.text: Putting the budget in front of approvers

Present the plan as a table of units, tier, quantity, unit range and total range, with separate rows for labour, power and reserve. Municipalities and BIAs can request line-item, RFP-ready quotes with net-30 invoicing and tax-exempt handling, which keeps the final number auditable. See the [commercial overview](/commercial) for property types, or go straight to the [shop](/shop) and add items to an inquiry cart to build your quote.

faq.q: How much should a BIA budget for holiday decorations?
faq.a: Budget by unit rather than by a lump sum. Count poles, trees and entrances, assign each a tier, and price from the ranges above, then add 20 to 35 percent for first-year installation and 8 to 12 percent annually for spares and repairs. Most BIAs phase the purchase over three seasons.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to buy or rent commercial Christmas decorations?
faq.a: Buying usually wins over three or more seasons, because commercial-grade aluminum-frame and LED pieces last many years with proper storage. Renting can suit a single-season event or a trial of a new location. If you do buy, plan storage space and a test routine from day one.

faq.q: What are the hidden costs of a commercial Christmas display?
faq.a: The big ones are install labour, bucket truck rental, electrician time for transformers and circuits, takedown, storage space and annual spares. Electricity itself is usually a small line for LED displays.

faq.q: How early should we order for a mid-November install?
faq.a: Submit your inquiry by September. Standard stock ships from London, Ontario, but larger 3D, overhead and custom-size items take longer, and installer crews book up in October.

faq.q: Can we get a formal quote for council or board approval?
faq.a: Yes. Submit an inquiry and the team replies by email with line-item pricing, shipping cost, timeline and any volume pricing. Municipalities and BIAs can also request net-30 invoicing and tax-exempt handling.
